question: A 64-year-old male farmer, ex-smoker (5 years old), COPD and rheumatoid arthritis in corticosteroid treatment. Consultation in the emergency room due to intense headache of 2 days of evolution with buccal commissure deviation. As an antecedent, he recounts that after a month of flu, cough persists, purulent expectoration and occasionally haemoptica, fever, anorexia, asthenia and weight loss. Upon arrival, there is a fever of 38.2ºC, multiple cutaneous abscesses in the hands, back and buttocks (some with fistulous trajectories) and right central facial paralysis, apical infiltrates with small pleural effusion associated with the chest x-ray and leukocytosis with neutrophilia. . Among the following suspected diagnoses, I would consider MOST probable:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Ex-smoker" -> "COPD" -> "chronic lung damage" -> "increased risk of infections" -> "persistent cough and purulent expectoration" -> "possible nocardiosis" -> "cutaneous abscesses" -> "fistulous trajectories" -> "right central facial paralysis" -> "nocardiosis affecting CNS" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Ex-smoker" -> "COPD" -> "chronic lung damage" -> "increased risk of infections" -> "persistent cough and purulent expectoration" -> "possible tuberculosis" -> "fever and weight loss" -> "cutaneous abscesses" -> "fistulous trajectories" -> "right central facial paralysis" -> "tuberculosis affecting CNS" -> 75%

CHAIN: "Ex-smoker" -> "COPD" -> "chronic lung damage" -> "increased risk of infections" -> "persistent cough and purulent expectoration" -> "possible pulmonary neoplasm" -> "fever and weight loss" -> "cutaneous abscesses" -> "fistulous trajectories" -> "right central facial paralysis" -> "brain metastases" -> 50%
analysis: The patient presents with a combination of symptoms including persistent cough with purulent expectoration, fever, weight loss, cutaneous abscesses, and right central facial paralysis. These symptoms, along with the history of corticosteroid use and immunosuppression due to rheumatoid arthritis, suggest an opportunistic infection. Nocardiosis is a bacterial infection caused by Nocardia species, which can cause pulmonary symptoms, cutaneous abscesses, and central nervous system involvement, including brain abscesses, especially in immunocompromised individuals. The presence of apical infiltrates and pleural effusion on the chest X-ray further supports a pulmonary infection. While disseminated tuberculosis could also present with similar symptoms, the cutaneous abscesses and the specific combination of symptoms are more characteristic of nocardiosis.
